Maladaptive Strategies.value: I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied
go over and over why the event happened to me
work excessively to avoid being alone with thoughts

Threat.value: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things

Negative Appraisals.value: I should have protected others and I failed
Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation
I am not sure my life is worth living anymore

vignette: Clara, a 40-year-old data scientist, sat at her desk, her fingers hovering over the keyboard while the glow of the screen illuminated her weary face. Married and living in a suburban area, she had always prided herself on her analytical prowess, but a traumatic incident had shattered her sense of control. Three years ago, she had witnessed a violent altercation between two groups in her town, one side comprised mostly of Arab villagers. The flames that erupted during the chaos had cast an eerie light, and the sounds of shouting and panic had etched themselves into her memory, leaving her feeling helpless. The vividness of that day resurfaced unexpectedly, often triggered by mundane moments—a flickering light, the crackling of a fire, or even the sight of an unfamiliar person on the street. The intensity of her memories often overwhelmed her, manifesting as flashbacks that left her feeling as though she were reliving the horror. "It’s as if I’m back there, watching everything unfold again," she would confide, her voice trembling. These intrusive memories not only heightened her perception of danger but also made her feel acutely vulnerable. Strangers now appeared threatening, their approach causing her anxiety to spike. Each time she stepped out, she would scan her surroundings, her heart racing at the sight of someone who bore no ill intent. This constant state of alertness seeped into her daily life, compelling Clara to overwork herself, pouring her energy into tasks that kept her mind occupied and away from the relentless cycle of thoughts that haunted her. Whenever she felt the familiar grip of anxiety tighten around her, she would dive deeper into her work, convinced that staying busy would shield her from the intrusive memories that threatened to resurface. With each passing day, Clara found solace in burying herself in work, believing that the busier she was, the less time she would have to ruminate on the event. Yet, this strategy backfired, as it only increased her feelings of isolation. "If I let myself think about it, I might not be able to get out of bed," she would think, justifying her excessive hours at the office. But even in her work, the memories would creep in, often triggered by the mere mention of conflict or the sight of fire in a presentation. The more she tried to escape her thoughts, the more they seemed to tighten around her, pulling her into a relentless spiral of self-doubt. Each time she felt the threat of her memories approaching, she would avoid situations that might trigger them, believing that by staying away, she could keep the danger at bay. Clara's internal narrative had shifted dramatically. Her ongoing efforts to control her environment through avoidance only reinforced her perception of threat, as she convinced herself that if she encountered reminders of the event, she might not be able to cope. She battled with the belief that she had failed to protect others during the incident. The guilt weighed heavily on her, leading her to constantly compare herself to others, convinced that someone else would have intervened effectively. "Why couldn’t I do something? Someone else would have acted differently," she would lament. This negative appraisal not only clouded her perception of herself but also intensified the clarity of her memories, making them feel more real and vivid than any other recollection. At times, she questioned the worth of her own life, grappling with the despair that came from feeling trapped in her past. As the months turned into years, the cycle continued, with her maladaptive strategies feeding back into her memories. Overworking herself would lead to moments of exhaustion, where the memories would flood back with full force, reminding her of the chaos she had witnessed. Each auditory recall—echoes of the cries and the flames—was a trigger, pushing her further into avoidance and isolation. The threat she felt from others and from her own mind kept her in a state of hypervigilance, where she would find herself checking locks multiple times before resting, a futile attempt to regain some semblance of control over her environment. "When a memory would resurface, reminding her of the chaos, she would bury herself deeper in work, believing that if she kept moving, she could avoid the intrusive thoughts that threatened to overwhelm her." Clara’s world had become smaller, her relationships strained by her inability to share the burden of her trauma. "The more she avoided confronting the places and situations that reminded her of the incident, the greater the sense of threat loomed in her mind, as if her avoidance confirmed that danger was still very real." She longed for relief but was terrified of confronting the pain that lay beneath the surface. "The avoidance had kept her from confronting the situation, allowing the threat to linger unabated, as no evidence had ever shown her that the world could be safe again." "The more she relived the memories of that day, the more she felt compelled to keep herself busy, believing that staying occupied would stave off the intrusive thoughts that threatened to pull her back into the chaos." It was this yearning for peace, coupled with the realization that her strategies were no longer working, that finally led her to seek help. "This avoidance strategy only reinforced her memories, as the more she suppressed her thoughts, the more vivid they became, lurking just beneath the surface, waiting for a moment of quiet to resurface." "With the ever-present sense of danger looming, she believed that planning her exits and checking the locks was not merely a habit, but a necessary precaution against an imminent threat." On the brink of despair, she knew she needed to confront her past, yet the fear of facing the memories haunted her. "The more she buried herself in work, the more the memories felt alive, and each effort to avoid them paradoxically made her feel the threat was still very real, as if her actions were confirming her fears." What frightened Clara most was the thought that perhaps, despite all her efforts, she might never feel whole again. "Her belief that she had failed to act created an unshakeable link to her memories, making them feel as though they were waiting for her to acknowledge them, reinforcing her sense of threat with every recollection." "The belief that she had failed to act during the incident kept pulling her back to that day, each reflection reinforcing the memory and making it more vivid, as if she were constantly replaying the moment she felt powerless." "After experiencing these intrusive memories, even the most ordinary sounds—a kettle whistling or a door slamming—felt like warnings she couldn't ignore, drawing her back into the anxiety of that day." "Her attempts to avoid thinking about the trauma left her unprepared for when the memories finally surfaced, making them feel louder and more oppressive than ever, as if they had been waiting for her to stop running." "Each place she avoided became a stark reminder of her trauma, mapping out a territory of fear that confined her more with every decision to stay away, until she felt trapped by her own self-imposed limitations." "Her avoidance of familiar routes and places only served to heighten her sense of threat, as each decision to stay away confirmed her belief that the world was still dangerous." "Each time she told herself she should have intervened, the memories became clearer and sharper, as if her guilt was sharpening the focus on the details of her perceived failure." "As the memories flooded back, she found herself retreating further into her work, convinced that by avoiding quiet moments, she could keep the memories at bay." "Each time a memory of the incident surfaced, the urgency to drown it out with work only intensified, as she thought staying busy would shield her from the unsettling feelings that accompanied those recollections." "Her belief that she had failed to protect others in that moment led her to replay the details of the incident in her mind, further sharpening the images and sounds, making them feel more immediate and haunting." "These spirals often led her to avoid quiet moments, as memories from the past would flood back, and she learned to keep distractions close at hand to stave off the onslaught." "Each time these triggers emerged, they would send her heart racing, amplifying her sense of threat and leaving her on high alert, as if danger was lurking just out of sight." "When the threat of anxiety felt too overwhelming, she would plan her day meticulously, believing that by controlling her environment, she could mitigate the danger that seemed ever-present." "Such recollections would prompt her to withdraw from social gatherings, convinced that the risk of encountering reminders of the chaos was too great to bear." "The continual avoidance had solidified her belief that the danger was real and ongoing, leaving her feeling trapped in a cycle where safety felt perpetually out of reach." "When the panic surged, she would bury herself in work, thinking that if she stayed busy, she could avoid those moments of overwhelming anxiety that accompanied the memories." "The belief that she had failed to protect others during the incident kept bringing her back to that moment, as if each reminder of her perceived weakness invited the memory to resurface, sharper and more distressing." "These memories would often overwhelm her, driving her to work harder, convinced that staying occupied could shield her from the painful recollections that threatened to erupt." vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette does not convey how triggers influence Clara's maladaptive strategies, such as overworking to avoid memories.
  e.g. "She stopped taking that route to work entirely — better to add twenty minutes to her commute than to feel that way again."
  e.g. "When the anniversary came around, she kept herself moving all day, cleaning, cooking, anything, because sitting still meant the thoughts would catch up."
  e.g. "She started leaving events early, telling herself she was tired, because staying too long meant the chances of something going wrong only multiplied."
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: The relationship between negative appraisals and memory is not established, as it does not show how Clara's beliefs affect her memories of the incident.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette lacks the connection that memories influence triggers for Clara, as it does not illustrate how her recollections prompt specific reminders.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Memory: There is no connection showing that maladaptive strategies lead to memory issues, as it does not link her coping mechanisms to the flooding of her memories.
  e.g. "She had been avoiding any mention of it for so long that when the memory finally surfaced, it was louder than it had ever been — all that suppression had kept it fresh."
  e.g. "Not talking about it meant the memory had never been put anywhere; it remained in her, undisturbed and intact, exactly where she had left it."
  e.g. "The effort of keeping it at a distance had paradoxically kept it close — she had thought about not thinking about it every day for three years."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: The vignette does not depict how maladaptive strategies influence triggers, as it does not clarify how her avoidance strategies relate to specific reminders.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Threat: The relationship indicating that maladaptive strategies lead to a sense of threat is missing, as it does not connect her coping methods to feelings of danger.
  e.g. "Never having stayed in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, her body had never received the evidence it needed — the threat remained as high as the day it was set."
  e.g. "The checking and the avoidance had kept her alive, in her nervous system's accounting, which meant the danger they were responding to must be real and ongoing."
  e.g. "Without ever testing the feeling, she had no way to know that the threat was not what her body insisted it was — the safety behaviours had sealed that possibility off."

vignette_attempts.vignette: Clara, a 40-year-old data scientist, sat at her desk, her fingers hovering over the keyboard while the glow of the screen illuminated her weary face. Married and living in a suburban area, she had always prided herself on her analytical prowess, but a traumatic incident had shattered her sense of control. Three years ago, she had witnessed a violent altercation between two groups in her town, one side comprised mostly of Arab villagers. The flames that erupted during the chaos had cast an eerie light, and the sounds of shouting and panic had etched themselves into her memory, leaving her feeling helpless. The vividness of that day resurfaced unexpectedly, often triggered by mundane moments—a flickering light, the crackling of a fire, or even the sight of an unfamiliar person on the street. The intensity of her memories often overwhelmed her, manifesting as flashbacks that left her feeling as though she were reliving the horror. "It’s as if I’m back there, watching everything unfold again," she would confide, her voice trembling. These intrusive memories not only heightened her perception of danger but also made her feel acutely vulnerable. Strangers now appeared threatening, their approach causing her anxiety to spike. Each time she stepped out, she would scan her surroundings, her heart racing at the sight of someone who bore no ill intent. This constant state of alertness seeped into her daily life, compelling Clara to overwork herself, pouring her energy into tasks that kept her mind occupied and away from the relentless cycle of thoughts that haunted her. With each passing day, Clara found solace in burying herself in work, believing that the busier she was, the less time she would have to ruminate on the event. Yet, this strategy backfired, as it only increased her feelings of isolation. "If I let myself think about it, I might not be able to get out of bed," she would think, justifying her excessive hours at the office. But even in her work, the memories would creep in, often triggered by the mere mention of conflict or the sight of fire in a presentation. The more she tried to escape her thoughts, the more they seemed to tighten around her, pulling her into a relentless spiral of self-doubt. Clara's internal narrative had shifted dramatically. She battled with the belief that she had failed to protect others during the incident. The guilt weighed heavily on her, leading her to constantly compare herself to others, convinced that someone else would have intervened effectively. "Why couldn’t I do something? Someone else would have acted differently," she would lament. This negative appraisal not only clouded her perception of herself but also intensified the clarity of her memories, making them feel more real and vivid than any other recollection. At times, she questioned the worth of her own life, grappling with the despair that came from feeling trapped in her past. As the months turned into years, the cycle continued, with her maladaptive strategies feeding back into her memories. Overworking herself would lead to moments of exhaustion, where the memories would flood back with full force, reminding her of the chaos she had witnessed. Each auditory recall—echoes of the cries and the flames—was a trigger, pushing her further into avoidance and isolation. The threat she felt from others and from her own mind kept her in a state of hypervigilance, where she would find herself checking locks multiple times before resting, a futile attempt to regain some semblance of control over her environment. "When a memory would resurface, reminding her of the chaos, she would bury herself deeper in work, believing that if she kept moving, she could avoid the intrusive thoughts that threatened to overwhelm her." Clara’s world had become smaller, her relationships strained by her inability to share the burden of her trauma. "The more she avoided confronting the places and situations that reminded her of the incident, the greater the sense of threat loomed in her mind, as if her avoidance confirmed that danger was still very real." She longed for relief but was terrified of confronting the pain that lay beneath the surface. "The avoidance had kept her from confronting the situation, allowing the threat to linger unabated, as no evidence had ever shown her that the world could be safe again." "The more she relived the memories of that day, the more she felt compelled to keep herself busy, believing that staying occupied would stave off the intrusive thoughts that threatened to pull her back into the chaos." It was this yearning for peace, coupled with the realization that her strategies were no longer working, that finally led her to seek help. "This avoidance strategy only reinforced her memories, as the more she suppressed her thoughts, the more vivid they became, lurking just beneath the surface, waiting for a moment of quiet to resurface." "With the ever-present sense of danger looming, she believed that planning her exits and checking the locks was not merely a habit, but a necessary precaution against an imminent threat." On the brink of despair, she knew she needed to confront her past, yet the fear of facing the memories haunted her. "The more she buried herself in work, the more the memories felt alive, and each effort to avoid them paradoxically made her feel the threat was still very real, as if her actions were confirming her fears." What frightened Clara most was the thought that perhaps, despite all her efforts, she might never feel whole again. "Her belief that she had failed to act created an unshakeable link to her memories, making them feel as though they were waiting for her to acknowledge them, reinforcing her sense of threat with every recollection." "The belief that she had failed to act during the incident kept pulling her back to that day, each reflection reinforcing the memory and making it more vivid, as if she were constantly replaying the moment she felt powerless." "After experiencing these intrusive memories, even the most ordinary sounds—a kettle whistling or a door slamming—felt like warnings she couldn't ignore, drawing her back into the anxiety of that day." "Her attempts to avoid thinking about the trauma left her unprepared for when the memories finally surfaced, making them feel louder and more oppressive than ever, as if they had been waiting for her to stop running." "Each place she avoided became a stark reminder of her trauma, mapping out a territory of fear that confined her more with every decision to stay away, until she felt trapped by her own self-imposed limitations." "Her avoidance of familiar routes and places only served to heighten her sense of threat, as each decision to stay away confirmed her belief that the world was still dangerous." "Each time she told herself she should have intervened, the memories became clearer and sharper, as if her guilt was sharpening the focus on the details of her perceived failure." "As the memories flooded back, she found herself retreating further into her work, convinced that by avoiding quiet moments, she could keep the memories at bay." "Each time a memory of the incident surfaced, the urgency to drown it out with work only intensified, as she thought staying busy would shield her from the unsettling feelings that accompanied those recollections." "Her belief that she had failed to protect others in that moment led her to replay the details of the incident in her mind, further sharpening the images and sounds, making them feel more immediate and haunting." "These spirals often led her to avoid quiet moments, as memories from the past would flood back, and she learned to keep distractions close at hand to stave off the onslaught." "Each time these triggers emerged, they would send her heart racing, amplifying her sense of threat and leaving her on high alert, as if danger was lurking just out of sight." "When the threat of anxiety felt too overwhelming, she would plan her day meticulously, believing that by controlling her environment, she could mitigate the danger that seemed ever-present." "Such recollections would prompt her to withdraw from social gatherings, convinced that the risk of encountering reminders of the chaos was too great to bear." "The continual avoidance had solidified her belief that the danger was real and ongoing, leaving her feeling trapped in a cycle where safety felt perpetually out of reach."
